title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
summary: Researchers introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of future signal evolution. They instantiate this principle in LOTUS, a model that combines raw patches with spectral representations and achieves top performance on TSRBench while using minimal trainable parameters. The approach enables compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size.
key_points: Researchers developed forecast grounding and LOTUS, a pretraining principle and model that maps time-series patches into the LLM embedding space to predict future evolution.
This method preserves critical temporal and spectral information, allowing compact models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size by 3.36% on TSRBench.

title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
summary: Researchers introduce a self-distillation technique using answer-only data for reasoning LLMs, training an inverse reasoning model to generate latent chain-of-thought sequences conditioned on answers. Evaluated on Qwen3-0.6B for Countdown and GSM8K tasks, this offline approach roughly doubles hard-prompt pass@1 performance after GRPO saturation and doubles as an accurate test-time verifier. The method bypasses the compute inefficiencies of reinforcement learning and the supervision bottlenecks of missing reasoning traces.

key_points: An inverse reasoning model was trained to generate chain-of-thought sequences conditioned solely on answer-only data as latent variables.
The approach doubles pass@1 on hard prompts after GRPO saturation and improves best-of-n test-time verification accuracy from 0.753 to 0.969 on Countdown.

title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
summary: This research evaluates nine representative class-incremental learning methods across five protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets to test their transferability from computer vision. The diagnostic benchmark reveals that vision-based CIL methods fail to transfer reliably due to weak gradient stability signals, heterogeneous embedding geometry, and mismatched covariance assumptions. These findings demonstrate that continual-learning design must adapt to the specific geometry of protein representations rather than treating encoders as passive feature extractors.
priority_explanation: Reports measured benchmark or evaluation results
key_points: Evaluated nine class-incremental learning methods across five protein encoders and two enzyme datasets, finding that no existing vision CIL method transfers reliably to protein sequence and structure encoders.
Identified root causes of failure including weak gradient-based stability signals, embedding geometry heterogeneity, and scaling mismatches in covariance assumptions.

title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
summary: This study evaluates whether machine-learning perturbation predictors can learn unseen gene interactions during out-of-distribution screening. The authors introduce additive disagreement (AD) as a metric to measure model deviation from simple additive predictions of single-gene effects. Across eight models and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform the additive baseline, and larger deviations from linearity correlate with higher prediction errors.
key_points: Evaluated eight machine-learning perturbation prediction models across three Perturb-seq datasets to test generalization on unseen gene combinations.
Showed that specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform a simple additive baseline, and higher additive disagreement correlates with greater prediction error.
Introduced additive disagreement as a robust confidence signal to guide decision-making in agentic perturbation-screening workflows.

title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
summary: Researchers introduce a token utility formulation for on-policy distillation derived directly from the distillation objective using the categorical Fisher matrix and logit gradients. Instantiated as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), the method applies continuous, mean-normalized token weighting that improves mathematical reasoning performance across multiple student-teacher pairs. The approach outperforms uniform on-policy distillation on mathematical reasoning benchmarks under both reverse-KL and forward-KL objectives.
priority_explanation: Reports measured benchmark or evaluation results
key_points: Derived a closed-form token utility for on-policy distillation based on the categorical Fisher matrix and logit gradients under a local KL budget.
Provides a principled way to perform continuous token weighting, termed Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), aligning token selection with the specific distillation objective.
Improves mathematical reasoning performance by 1.08 to 4.0 macro points across Qwen3 student-teacher pairs compared to uniform on-policy distillation.

title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
summary: Researchers introduce PMO-Dock, a standardized benchmark and protocol for docking-based molecular optimization featuring 25 tasks across hit generation, lead optimization, and specificity testing. The evaluation framework enforces strict oracle budgets and separates validation tasks from held-out test tasks to measure true generalization and sample efficiency. Benchmarking four distinct optimization methods reveals that no single approach dominates universally across all tasks, highlighting the necessity for method-dependent selection strategies in drug discovery.
priority_explanation: Reports measured benchmark or evaluation results
key_points: PMO-Dock was introduced as a standardized benchmark and evaluation protocol consisting of 25 tasks for docking-based molecular optimization.
The benchmark matters because it establishes a rigorous framework with strict oracle budgets and held-out test tasks to evaluate generalization and sample efficiency reliably.

title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
summary: Researchers examine data density scaling laws for image self-distillation models across multiple datasets including ImageNet, Waymo, and Ego4D. They demonstrate that sample repetition can sometimes outperform training on larger unique sample sets, challenging conventional scaling assumptions. A modified Chinchilla-style scaling law is proposed to account for unique samples and sample repetition.
key_points: Repeated training on smaller random subsets of image data can outperform training on larger unique sample sets for self-distillation models.
A modified Chinchilla-style scaling law is introduced to account for unique sample counts and repetition factors in data-compute trade-offs.

title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
summary: Researchers introduce an automated layout generator and a fast open-source approximate ray tracer to produce 128 million synthetic indoor radio-map samples. Pretraining ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders on this synthetic data reduces downstream prediction error by 15% across five indoor tasks. The findings demonstrate predictable power-law data-scaling trends for radio-map prediction using cheap simulated data.
key_points: A new pipeline generates 128M synthetic indoor radio-map samples using an automated layout generator and a fast approximate ray tracer.
Pretrained ResNet-101 models achieve a 15% average error reduction on indoor radio-map prediction tasks and display reliable power-law data-scaling trends.

title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
summary: The authors introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts for Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) that dynamically determines per-token rank allocation using a robust noise-floor threshold and Stein's unbiased risk estimate. SQUELCH eliminates cross-talk noise and redundant components without adding trainable parameters, improving performance across commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE tasks using LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3.
priority_explanation: Reports measured benchmark or evaluation results
key_points: SQUELCH was introduced as a router-free mixture of rank-one LoRA experts that soft-thresholds token responses against a robust noise floor determined by Stein's unbiased risk estimate.

It improves performance by 2.2-3.2 points over standard LoRA and 0.8-1.2 points over mixture baselines while activating an average of only 8.6 out of 32 components per token, adding zero trainable parameters.
Machine learning researchers and practitioners deploying models like LLaMA, Qwen, and DeBERTaV3 with LoRA adaptation are directly affected.
